summary: Compare and order numbers through 120 using >, = and < grounded in place value: start with the highest relevant place, checking hundreds first across 100, then tens and ones when higher places tie. Establish quantity and number-line meaning before symbols. Use two-digit pairs, same-tens ties, and sets such as 98, 104, 111 and 120. Tens-first is valid for the two-digit examples only; a zero tens digit in 104 does not make it smaller than 98.
misconceptions: Using the crocodile/Pac-Man mouth as a rote trick with no sense of which number is actually bigger, so the symbol is placed by guess.
Compares the ones first, or treats the tens digit as the leading place across 100 (e.g. putting 98 above 104 because 9 is greater than 0), instead of checking hundreds before tens and ones.
Reversing the symbol — knowing which is bigger but writing > where < belongs.
Thinking = can only sit between identical-looking expressions, not that it asserts equal value.
For two-digit same-tens pairs, for same-tens pairs, defaulting to 'they're the same' because the tens match, instead of moving to the ones.

activities.title: Comparison bench: build, see, and place the symbol
steps: Build or show two two-digit numbers in two forms at once: base-ten block piles and dots/markers on a shared 0-100 number line.

Decide which is greater by looking at the quantity/position first (more tens rods and more blocks in total, further right on the line), then say it aloud: e.g. 'forty-three is greater than thirty-four'.
Place the correct symbol (<, >, or =) into the gap between the two numbers.
Read the completed statement both ways: 34 < 43 ('thirty-four is less than forty-three') and 43 > 34 ('forty-three is greater than thirty-four').
For these two-digit pairs, state the rule: compare tens first and compare ones only if tens are equal. Explain that across 100 the hundreds place must be checked before tens.
activities.insight: 'Greater' and 'less' name a real difference in quantity/position, and the symbol records that relation — the same fact can be read from either end.

activities.title: Tens-tie rounds: when the first digit can't decide
steps: Compare same-tens pairs such as 34 and 38, where the tens columns are identical.
Notice that the tens no longer settle it, then compare the ones to decide which is greater.
Place the correct symbol and justify: 'the tens are the same, so I looked at the ones'.
Try a 'crossed-decade' pair such as 52 and 48, and check: 52 has more tens, so it is greater even though its ones digit (2) is smaller than 8.
Also handle an equal pair such as 60 and 60, choosing = and explaining that both show the same value.
activities.insight: For two-digit numbers, compare tens first and let ones decide only when tens tie. For numbers across 100, check hundreds before either of those places. The equals sign asserts equal value, not merely similar-looking symbols.

activities.title: Order a scrambled set onto a washing line
steps: Order a two-digit set such as 19, 27, 51 and 72, then order a set spanning 100 such as 98, 104, 111 and 120, from smallest to largest.
Repeat, ordering the same set largest to smallest.
Include a set containing a same-tens tie so ordering requires the ones to break it.
Check the finished order left to right and record the relations with symbols where appropriate.
Explain the order using the highest relevant place first: hundreds across 100, then tens and ones as needed.
activities.insight: Ordering a set applies the highest-place-value comparison rule repeatedly: hundreds before tens before ones, using only the places needed for each pair.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'how do you know?'
steps: Explain aloud which digit you looked at first and why, on a tricky pair such as 52 and 48.
Answer: '34 and 43 use the same two digits — how can one be bigger?' by referring to place value.
Decide and justify the symbol for an equal pair like 60 and 60.
activities.insight: Justifying comparisons reveals the place-value reasoning behind the symbol: tens first for two-digit pairs, and hundreds first when crossing 100.

activities.title: Consolidation and check: choose, order, fill the gap
steps: Choose the correct symbol between varied pairs, including a two-digit same-tens pair, a symbol-reversal lure, and a pair crossing 100 such as 98 and 104.
Order a scrambled set smallest to largest.
Fill in the missing symbol in a statement and read it back aloud.
activities.insight: The highest-place-value comparison rule and correct symbol use apply across two-digit pairs and numbers through 120.

checkQuestion: Watch them compare and order. 'Put the right symbol between 34 and 43. Now order these smallest to largest: 27, 72, 19, 51. Tell me how you decided.' The 34/43 pair (same digits) is the key — watch whether they weigh the tens first. Then order 98, 104, 111 and 120. Put comparison symbols between 98 and 104, 104 and 111, and 104 and 104, and explain which place decides each comparison.
checkAnswer: 34 < 43; order 19, 27, 51, 72; and for these two-digit comparisons they check tens first, with ones breaking a tie. Across 100: 98 < 104 < 111 < 120; 98 < 104, 104 < 111, and 104 = 104. Compare the highest relevant place first: hundreds, then tens, then ones.
